title: Reinforcement Learning from Denoising Feedback

paper.title: Reinforcement Learning from Denoising Feedback
paper.abstract: Abstract Policy loss estimation remains a fundamental and long-standing challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) for diffusion language models (dLLMs). We introduce Reinforcement Learning from Denoising Feedback (RLDF) , a novel training paradigm that leverages feedback obtained from rollout and training processes to facilitate accurate and efficient policy loss estimation. To balance the trade-off between computational efficiency and estimation effectiveness, RLDF optimizes the model toward the clipped clean state x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} from intermediate noisy states x t x_{t} , combined with weighted timestep sampling over t t . Extensive experiments demonstrate that RLDF achieves consistent and substantial improvements in both performance and generalizability across two representative dLLM architectures, LLaDA and Dream, on multiple reasoning benchmarks. Our work lays a principled foundation for scalable reinforcement learning in diffusion language models. We build Drift , a training framework for dLLMs, available at https://github.com/ant-research/Drift .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent breakthroughs in diffusion language models (DLMs) ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) , such as Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) and LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) , have positioned them as a promising pathway toward highly capable foundation models ( Google DeepMind, 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Khanna et al., 2025 ) . The appeal of DLMs ( Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023 ; Yu et al., 2025b ) stems from several intrinsic advantages over autoregressive (AR) architectures: bidirectional attention ( Gong et al., 2025 ) , arbitrary decoding order, and the potential for multi-token parallel generation ( Wu et al., 2025b ; Wu et al., 2025a ) . Nevertheless, DLMs currently underperform their autoregressive counterparts across many benchmarks, a gap largely attributable to immature training methodologies and pipelines. Among the capabilities most in need of improvement, reasoning ( OpenAI, 2024 ; Anthropic, 2025 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) stands out as particularly critical. Reasoning of language models is a frontier that has been extensively explored and substantially advanced within the autoregressive paradigm. Reinforcement learning (RL) ( Kaelbling et al., 1996 ) has emerged as an effective and highly generalizable approach for cultivating reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs). Evolving from PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) through DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , and subsequent variants ( Yu et al., 2025a ; Yue et al., 2025 ) , RL has consistently improved LLM reasoning with verifiable reward ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Uesato et al., 2022 ) across diverse scenarios, including tool use ( Jin et al., 2025 ) , mathematics ( Snell et al., 2024 ) , and code generation ( Le et al., 2022 ; Shojaee et al., 2023 ) . However, these RL methods cannot be directly transplanted to diffusion language models due to two fundamental discrepancies: the attention mechanism (causal vs. bidirectional) and the generative process (next-token prediction vs. full-sequence denoising). A central obstacle in adapting RL to DLMs lies in policy loss estimation . In autoregressive models, the policy loss is obtained through a single forward pass under causal attention. In contrast, the arbitrary decoding order and bidirectional attention of DLMs render exact log-likelihood computation intractable. Prior approaches ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Ou et al., 2025 ) approximate the policy loss via either no-masking or random-masking schemes, both of which introduce a substantial mismatch between training and inference. Alternatively, computing the policy loss at every denoising step ( Ni et al., 2026 ) preserves train–inference alignment but incurs prohibitive computational and time costs due to the iterative nature of the denoising process. This exposes a core challenge: how to balance the fidelity of policy loss estimation against its computational cost. To address this challenge, we propose Reinforcement Learning from Denoising Feedback (RLDF) , a training paradigm that leverages two complementary feedback sources. Rollout feedback captures unmasking probabilities and their corresponding timesteps along the denoising trajectory. Training feedback , derived from predicted probabilities during denoising training, provides signals from which we retain only the most informative positions for stable and effective policy updates. Building on these signals, we employ a weighted sampling strategy ( Rubinstein and Kroese, 2016 ) that preferentially selects denoising steps with high predictive uncertainty ( Choi et al., 2022 ) —those exerting the greatest influence on the final generation. The policy loss is computed exclusively over these selected steps, yielding a favorable precision–efficiency trade-off while remaining compatible with diverse masking strategies and readily extensible to emerging training schemes. Empirical results demonstrate that our method exhibits substantial improvements on math and code tasks across both LLaDA and Dream models, as shown in Table 2 . Furthermore, our approach achieves faster convergence rates with more precise policy gradient estimation. We also demonstrate the advantage of leveraging the clean state rather than the next state for loss estimation, which avoids loss spikes and improves the utilization of training signals. In summary, our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We open-source Drift , an extensible and modular RL framework purpose-built for dLLMs, to facilitate community research and novel algorithms. • We propose an improved policy loss estimation method that achieves a better trade-off between efficiency and precision. • We unlock the reasoning potential of dLLMs (LLaDA and Dream), providing empirical insights for dLLM community.

sections.heading: 2.1 Diffusion Language Model
sections.text: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have evolved significantly, spanning approaches from continuous ( Li et al., 2022 ; Dieleman et al., 2022 ) to discrete domains ( Hoogeboom et al., 2021 ) . Recently, masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) define a text generation paradigm in which the output is produced through an iterative denoising process over discrete token sequences ( Austin et al., 2021 ) . In contrast to autoregressive models, which generate tokens sequentially from left to right, dLLMs employ bidirectional attention mechanisms and perform predictions across all token positions at each forward pass. Recent advances in training methodology have yielded a number of capable dLLM foundation models, including LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) , which is trained from scratch via full pre-training, and Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , which is obtained by adapting the pretrained Qwen2.5-7B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) to the diffusion framework.

sections.heading: 2.2 Reasoning in Diffusion Language Models
sections.text: Reasoning has long been a central topic in language model research. Diffusion language models have recently demonstrated promising potential across a range of reasoning tasks. The models show superiority in planning tasks ( Ye et al., 2024a ; Huang et al., 2025 ) and demonstrate better data learning efficiency ( Ni et al., 2025 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ) . Complementary lines of work have explored augmenting reasoning capabilities through established techniques such as chain-of-thought prompting ( Ye et al., 2024b ) , leveraging both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Austin et al., 2021 ) to elicit more structured and reliable inference. Further efforts have focused on accelerating the reasoning process ( Xie et al., 2025 ) , while others have investigated the design of remasking strategies to improve generation quality ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 2.3 Reinforcement Learning
sections.text: Reinforcement learning (RL) ( Kaelbling et al., 1996 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) , especially GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , has proven effective in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) ( He et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2025 ) . However, owing to fundamental differences in attention mechanisms and forward computation processes, diffusion language models require distinct strategies for computing RL losses. Existing loss computation methods have undergone successive refinements, evolving from Diffu-GRPO ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) through Coupled-GRPO ( Xie et al., 2025 ) to ELBO ( Ou et al., 2025 ) , etc. Each of these methods attempts to better align the training objective with the denoising nature of diffusion models. Nevertheless, all of these methods suffer from training-inference mismatch to varying degrees, which undermines the reliability of policy gradient estimation and ultimately limits reasoning performance. We are motivated by this limitation and propose a novel loss computation method that considers both accuracy and efficiency, serving as a stronger foundation for reinforcement learning on diffusion language models.

sections.heading: 3.2 Training Techniques
sections.text: Following the masked language modeling paradigm of BERT, MDMs are trained via random masking. Specifically, a parametric model p θ ( ⋅ ∣ x t ) p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t}) takes the partially masked sequence x t x_{t} as input and simultaneously predicts all masked tokens (denoted as 𝙼 \mathtt{M} ). It is optimized via a cross-entropy loss computed exclusively over the masked positions: ℒ ( θ ) ≜ − 𝔼 t , x 0 , x t [ 1 t ∑ i = 1 L 𝟙 [ x t , i = 𝐌 ] log p θ ( x 0 , i ∣ x t ) ] . \mathcal{L}(\theta)\triangleq-\mathbb{E}_{t,\,x_{0},\,x_{t}}\left[\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\mathds{1}[x_{t,i}=\mathbf{M}]\log p_{\theta}(x_{0,i}\mid x_{t})\right]. (2) However, a fundamental discrepancy exists between the training and denoising processes. During training, masking is applied randomly and independently across token positions, whereas during denoising, the set of masked positions evolves deterministically across steps based on model confidence. This mismatch results in substantially different masking patterns and contextual inputs between the two phases, leading to inconsistent attention distributions and key-value representations. Such train-inference discrepancy poses a significant challenge for reasoning-oriented fine-tuning, as the model is optimized under a distribution of masked contexts that poorly reflects those encountered at inference time.

sections.heading: 3.3 Challenges in Log Probability Estimation
sections.text: Unlike autoregressive models, whose loss can be computed within a single forward pass, diffusion language models do not enjoy this benefit due to their bidirectional attention mechanism. Specifically, the key-value (KV) representations change across denoising steps, making the forward computation distinct at each step. Early methods such as d1 ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) and wd1 ( Tang et al., 2025 ) adopt a full-sequence loss strategy, which computes the average loss over all token positions conditioned on the prompt only in a single forward pass: ℒ full-seq ​ ( o ∣ q ) = log ⁡ p θ ​ ( o ∣ q , o T ) . \mathcal{L}_{\text{full-seq}}(o\mid q)=\log p_{\theta}(o\mid q,o_{T}). However, all of these methods compute the loss under a context that is inconsistent with the actual rollout conditions at inference time, giving rise to a fundamental training-inference mismatch that undermines the reliability of policy gradient estimation in RL training.

sections.heading: 4.1 Denoising Feedback of Diffusion Models
sections.text: The denoising process of diffusion models contains rich information that can substantially benefit reinforcement learning. We extract feedback from two complementary stages: the rollout process and the training process . During rollout, we collect reasoning trajectories together with their timestep probabilities, which capture the reasoning context and guide the timestep selection. During training, we predict the clean state x 0 x_{0} from the noisy state x t x_{t} and derive the learning signal from the processed x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} through token-level clipping. Both sources of feedback are effective in stabilizing training, yet have been largely overlooked in prior paradigms.

sections.heading: 4.2 Loss Estimation at Timestep t
sections.text: To faithfully replicate the context in which each position is unmasked, we adopt a stepwise loss estimation scheme that enables precise gradient estimation without approximation. Formally, given a prompt q q and the sequence of tokens decoded across denoising timesteps o T , … , o 0 o_{T},\ldots,o_{0} , at each timestep t t we compute the forward process p ⁡ ( o 0 ∣ q , o t ) p(o_{0}\mid q,o_{t}) and evaluate the loss exclusively on the positions masked at timestep t t . This procedure exactly mirrors the model’s rollout without introducing any approximation error. However, this exact formulation incurs substantial computational overhead. Specifically, the number of forward passes scales linearly with the number of decoding steps n n , as the loss must be computed iteratively for each step. In practice, a standard reasoning trajectory requires approximately 256 decoding steps, resulting in 256 forward passes per sample and rendering naive stepwise training prohibitively expensive in both time and memory. sections.heading: 4.3 Weighted Sampling for Timestep Selection
sections.text: To mitigate the computational bottleneck, we propose selectively sampling a subset of denoising steps for loss computation rather than processing all steps exhaustively, adopting weighted sampling as the principled mechanism for timestep selection. Prior work has shown that entropy serves as an effective guidance signal during training ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) . As shown in Table 1 , distribution entropy and token probability at each position exhibit near-perfect correlation across both models and tasks, indicating that decoding probability is a faithful proxy for entropy. We therefore adopt per-step decoding probability as the weight for timestep selection, which not only provides a more intuitive perceptual signal but also avoids explicit entropy computation. As illustrated in Figure 2(a) , the distribution of per-token decoding probabilities is heavily skewed: the vast majority of tokens are decoded with high confidence (typically above 0.9), while only a small fraction are assigned low probability. Crucially, these low-confidence tokens exert disproportionate influence on the diversity of reasoning trajectories and exhibit strong correlation with final answer accuracy. As shown in Figure 2(b) , such tokens are often connective words in math and instruction verbs in code tasks. We therefore preferentially sample steps with lower average token confidence for loss computation. For diffusion language models, this sampling strategy offers a two-fold benefit: it substantially reduces the number of loss computation iterations, while simultaneously concentrating gradient signal on the most informative denoising steps, yielding a lower-variance and more rollout-faithful training objective.

sections.heading: Data and Models.
sections.text: Mathematical reasoning and code generation are widely adopted benchmarks for evaluating the reasoning capabilities of large language models. Accordingly, we conduct training and evaluation on both domains. For mathematical reasoning, we use the official training split of MATH ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) for training, and evaluate on MATH500 ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) , GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , and AMC23 ( Art of Problem Solving, 2023 ) . For code generation, we train on the training split of MBPP and evaluate on MBPP and HumanEval. We adopt two mainstream diffusion language models as our backbones: LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: Our training procedure consists solely of reinforcement learning, initialized from the pretrained diffusion backbones. For policy loss estimation, we apply weighted sampling over 16 denoising timesteps. To prevent excessive deviation from the reference model, we adopt the widely used k 3 k_{3} estimator for the KL regularization term. During rollout, we follow Wang et al. (2025b) and employ block-wise decoding with KV-cache to accelerate generation. Full hyperparameter and implementation details are provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: To highlight the generalization ability of each RL method, we adopt a strict cross-setting evaluation protocol: each model is trained on a single dataset with a fixed generation length of 256, and then evaluated across all remaining settings. Following prior work, we benchmark all models at generation lengths of 128, 256, and 512 under the dynamic and static sampling strategy. We compare our method against several well-established baselines, including d1 ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) (NeurIPS 2025), ESPO ( Ou et al., 2025 ) (ICLR 2026), TraceRL ( Wang et al., 2025b ) (ICLR 2026), and Coupled-GRPO ( Gong et al., 2025 ) (ICLR 2026). In addition, for the LLaDA series, we report the performance of LLaDA-1.5 ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) as an additional reference point.

sections.heading: Strong Performance Across Tasks and Models.
sections.text: Our reinforcement learning from denoising feedback (RLDF) method achieves consistently dominant performance across both LLaDA and Dream models on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, as reported in Table 2 . Nearly all configurations of our approach rank first or second among all baselines, with first-place results in the majority of settings. Notably, the performance gains are consistent across both model families, in contrast to d1 and ESPO, which demonstrate competitive results only on individual models. Relative to the respective base models, our approach yields substantial improvements of up to 10 accuracy points on Dream for MATH500 and MBPP, and approximately 8 points for LLaDA on the same benchmarks. These empirical results provide compelling evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed method.

sections.heading: Unlocking the Reasoning Potential of the Dream Model.
sections.text: An unexpected finding is that the Dream model converges remarkably rapidly during reinforcement learning, requiring only approximately 100 training steps on both math and code tasks. We hypothesize that this unexpectedly fast emergence of reasoning stems from latent capabilities inherited from the underlying Qwen architecture ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , which may have been suppressed during the adaptation from autoregressive to masked diffusion modeling. Our reinforcement learning procedure effectively reactivates these dormant reasoning capacities, recovering and amplifying the model’s problem-solving abilities. We further observe that training on Dream exhibits greater instability compared to LLaDA, manifesting as rapidly escalating KL divergence; we address this by applying a higher KL penalty coefficient ( β = 0.04 \beta=0.04 ). This instability may reflect a fundamental discontinuity introduced by the autoregressive-to-diffusion adaptation, pointing to a potential limitation of such model conversion approaches.

sections.heading: Cross-dataset generalization.
sections.text: Our method generalizes consistently across benchmarks, whereas competing methods often improve on one distribution at the cost of others. Specifically, it yields stable gains on out-of-distribution benchmarks including GSM8K, AMC23, and HumanEval. This is particularly notable for the shift from MBPP to HumanEval: MBPP describes function implementations in free-form natural language, while HumanEval requires completing partially defined function stubs under explicit constraints. The strong cross-dataset performance suggests that our models acquire transferable reasoning skills rather than overfitting to surface patterns of the training data.

sections.heading: Robustness to unmasking strategy.
sections.text: Our main experiments use a dynamic unmasking threshold (set to 0.9 0.9 ). To further test robustness, we evaluate each model under a static unmasking strategy across varying generation lengths and step counts, constraining the model to unmask one token per step and reporting results at 128, 256, and 512 steps in Table 3 . The static results largely mirror the trends observed under dynamic unmasking, and our method remains dominant particularly on Dream models. sections.heading: 6.1 Effect of Sampling Numbers and Temperature
sections.text: We investigate the effect of varying the number of sampling timesteps in Figure 3 . As expected, increasing the number of sampling timesteps accelerates convergence, analogous to the effect of increasing batch size. Since each additional sampling timestep introduces an extra forward and backward pass, a larger number of timesteps directly increases per-iteration training time. In our implementation, using 16 sampling steps incurs a computation cost comparable to that of the rollout process alone. We further observe that the sampling temperature has a notable impact on training stability, with lower temperatures yielding more stable training dynamics. A higher temperature corresponds to a more uniform selection across timesteps, whereas a lower temperature biases sampling toward low-entropy timesteps. We attribute this, in part, to the behavior of loss estimation. High-entropy timesteps contain fewer tokens, but each token carries critical learning signal; however, their limited quantity makes the loss estimation inherently unstable. In contrast, low-entropy timesteps involve substantially more tokens, providing a larger collection for averaging, though they require probability-based filtering to isolate the informative training signal from low-value tokens. This reveals a signal-noise trade-off: sufficient signal is required for stable optimization, yet noise from low-entropy timesteps must not dominate the loss estimation. Consequently, choosing an appropriate probability filtering threshold is crucial for training stability. Figure 3: Ablation on sequential remasking strategy. Mean rollout reward under varying remasking counts and timestep sampling temperatures. Larger remasking counts and lower sampling temperatures consistently lead to higher rollout rewards.

sections.heading: 6.2 Why 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} Estimation Outperforms 𝐱 t − 1 \mathbf{x}_{t-1} Estimation
sections.text: Theoretically, the one-step posterior can be recovered by marginalizing over the clean signal ( Austin et al., 2021 ) : p θ ​ ( x t − 1 ∣ x t ) = ∑ x 0 p θ ​ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) ​ q ​ ( x t − 1 ∣ x t , x 0 ) , p_{\theta}(x_{t-1}\mid x_{t})=\sum_{x_{0}}p_{\theta}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})\,q(x_{t-1}\mid x_{t},x_{0}), (12) so any x t − 1 x_{t-1} -prediction model implicitly commits to a particular path through x 0 x_{0} space, while x 0 x_{0} -prediction retains the full distribution over clean sequences. Predicting x 0 x_{0} thus exposes the model to a global denoising objective at every timestep, yielding a richer signal and a target distribution whose statistics remain stable across noise levels. This gap is amplified in practice. Under dynamic unmasking, tokens are revealed only when their probability exceeds a threshold (with a single token unmasked otherwise), so the supervisory signal for x t − 1 x_{t-1} -estimation is severely limited, especially when high-entropy timesteps are preferentially sampled. As shown empirically in Table 4 , x 0 x_{0} -estimation leverages ∼ \sim 15% of response tokens per sample, while x t − 1 x_{t-1} -estimation uses only ∼ \sim 2%, discarding most of the available signal. As is shown in Figure 4 , 𝐱 t − 1 \mathbf{x}_{t-1} -based estimation also exhibits pronounced KL loss spikes during training, attributable to the instability introduced by computing KL divergence over such a limited token set; the policy loss suffers from the same issue. In contrast, 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} -based estimation yields consistently higher rollout rewards, empirically confirming the superiority of clean state estimation for stable and effective training.

Without token clipping, both gradient norm and loss diverge by several orders of magnitude. At each training iteration, the model performs a forward pass conditioned on the partially observed context at timestep t t . Due to the limited context available, the model struggles to make reliable predictions for positions at timesteps t ′ ≪ t t^{\prime}\ll t , often assigning extremely low probabilities to those tokens. Under the loss formulation in Equation ( 8 ), these near-zero probabilities can dominate the loss computation, overshadowing the gradient signal from high-confidence tokens — precisely those from which we seek to learn. This imbalance inflates the noise-to-signal ratio and distorts the training dynamics. To increase the proportion of useful gradient signal in the policy loss, we apply token clipping by discarding clean state tokens whose predicted probability falls below a threshold (set to 0.2 in implementation). sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we address the fundamental challenge of log-likelihood estimation in the policy gradient objective of diffusion language models. We propose RLDF (Reinforcement Learning from Denoising Feedback), a principled method that achieves a favorable trade-off between estimation precision and computational efficiency by approximating the policy loss on clipped final states across a subset of selected timesteps t. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate both the effectiveness and the necessity of our approach in enabling stable and performant reinforcement learning for dLLMs. Furthermore, we introduce a comprehensive and extensible RL training framework Drift for dLLMs, encompassing flexible masking strategies and diverse training methodologies, with native compatibility for the two most prominent dLLM architectures, LLaDA and Dream.

sections.heading: Appendix A Classic Variants of Policy Loss
sections.text: We introduce three prevalent methods for policy loss estimation, derived from the no masking, random masking, and sequential masking perspectives, respectively. For brevity, we define the per-token importance ratio as r t , i ​ ( θ ) = ϕ π θ ​ ( o 0 , i ∣ c ) ϕ π θ old ​ ( o 0 , i ∣ c ) , r_{t,i}(\theta)\;=\;\frac{\phi_{\pi_{\theta}}(o_{0,i}\mid c)}{\phi_{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}}(o_{0,i}\mid c)}, (14) where the conditioning context c c varies across the three variants: c = q c=q for no masking, c = ( q , o ℳ i ) c=(q,\,o^{\mathcal{M}_{i}}) for random masking, and c = ( q , o t ) c=(q,\,o_{t}) for sequential masking. For all three objectives, A i k A_{i}^{k} denotes the token-level advantage, ε \varepsilon is the PPO clipping threshold, and β \beta controls the strength of the KL regularization toward the reference policy π ref \pi_{\text{ref}} . By convention, quantities without an explicit subscript t t correspond to the final step t = T t=T (e.g., r i ≜ r 0 , i r_{i}\triangleq r_{0,i} , o i ≜ o 0 , i o_{i}\triangleq o_{0,i} ).

sections.heading: All Masking.
sections.text: Diffu-GRPO ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) computes the policy-gradient loss over all tokens of every sampled response. For each query q q , a randomly masked variant q ′ q^{\prime} is constructed and used as the conditioning context, providing a one-step likelihood estimation at every position k ∈ { 1 , … , | o i | } k\in\{1,\dots,|o_{i}|\} : ℒ diffu ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 [ 1 G ∑ b = 1 G 1 | o b | ∑ i = 1 | o b | min ( r i ( b ) A i ( b ) , clip ( r i ( b ) , − ε , + ε ) A i ( b ) ) − β 𝔻 KL [ ϕ π θ ∥ ϕ π ref ] ] . \begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\text{diffu}}(\theta)=\ &\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\frac{1}{G}\!\sum_{b=1}^{G}\!\frac{1}{|o^{b}|}\!\sum_{i=1}^{|o^{b}|}\!\min\!\Big(r_{i}^{(b)}A_{i}^{(b)},\text{clip}(r_{i}^{(b)},1\!-\!\varepsilon,1\!+\!\varepsilon)A_{i}^{(b)}\Big)-\beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}\big[\phi_{\pi_{\theta}}\,\|\,\phi_{\pi_{\text{ref}}}\big]\Bigg].\end{split} (15) The expectation is taken over q ∼ 𝒟 q\sim\mathcal{D} , and { o i } i = 1 G ∼ π θ old ( ⋅ ∣ q ) \{o_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(\cdot\mid q) . Because the loss is averaged uniformly over | o i | |o_{i}| tokens, every output position contributes equally regardless of whether it was actually denoised at that step.

sections.text: Instead of scoring all tokens, random masking restricts the loss to a randomly sampled mask set ℳ b ⊆ { 1 , … , | o ( b ) | } \mathcal{M}_{b}\subseteq\{1,\dots,|o^{(b)}|\} for each response, while the unmasked tokens o ℳ b ¯ o^{{\overline{\mathcal{M}_{b}}}} and prompt q q serve as the context. This corresponds to a Monte-Carlo estimator of the masked-diffusion ELBO at the token level: ℒ ELBO ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 [ 1 G ∑ b = 1 G 1 | ℳ b | ∑ i ∈ ℳ b min ( r i ( b ) A i ( b ) , clip ( r i ( b ) , − ε , + ε ) A i ( b ) ) − β 𝔻 KL [ ϕ π θ ∥ ϕ π ref ] ] . \begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\text{ELBO}}(\theta)=\ &\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\frac{1}{G}\!\sum_{b=1}^{G}\!\frac{1}{|{\mathcal{M}}_{b}|}\!\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{M}}_{b}}\!\min\!\Big(r_{i}^{(b)}A_{i}^{(b)},\text{clip}(r_{i}^{(b)},1\!-\!\varepsilon,1\!+\!\varepsilon)A_{i}^{(b)}\Big)-\beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}\big[\phi_{\pi_{\theta}}\,\|\,\phi_{\pi_{\text{ref}}}\big]\Bigg].\end{split} (16) The expectation is taken over q ∼ 𝒟 q\sim\mathcal{D} , { o ( b ) } b = 1 G ∼ π θ old ( ⋅ ∣ q ) \{o^{(b)}\}_{b=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(\cdot\mid q) , and ℳ b ∼ masking ​ ( o ( b ) ) \mathcal{M}_{b}\sim\text{masking}(o^{(b)}) . By conditioning on the visible tokens and supervising only the masked positions, ELBO yields a lower-variance, theoretically grounded surrogate that is consistent with the training objective of masked diffusion language models. ESPO ( Ou et al., 2025 ) is modified from the ELBO estimation.

sections.heading: Sequential Masking.
sections.text: The sequential masking method further aligns the RL signal with the actual generation process by following the diffusion denoising trajectory τ = ( o T , o T − 1 , … , o 0 ) \tau=(o_{T},o_{T-1},\dots,o_{0}) , where o T o_{T} denotes the fully masked initial state and o 0 = o o_{0}=o is the final clean response. At each denoising timestep t t , the policy unmasks a subset of positions ℐ t \mathcal{I}_{t} conditioned on the partially denoised state o t o_{t} , producing the next state o t − 1 o_{t-1} . The loss is computed at exactly those positions: ℒ τ ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 [ 1 G ∑ b = 1 G 1 T ∑ t = 1 T 1 | ℐ t ( b ) | ∑ i ∈ ℐ t ( b ) min ( r t , i ( b ) A i ( b ) , clip ( r t , i ( b ) , − ε , + ε ) A t , i ( b ) ) − β 𝔻 KL [ ϕ π θ ∥ ϕ π ref ] ] . \begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\tau}(\theta)=\ &\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\frac{1}{G}\!\sum_{b=1}^{G}\!\frac{1}{T}\!\sum_{t=1}^{T}\!\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}^{(b)}_{t}|}\!\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}^{(b)}_{t}}\!\min\!\Big(r_{t,i}^{(b)}A_{i}^{(b)},\text{clip}(r_{t,i}^{(b)},1\!-\!\varepsilon,1\!+\!\varepsilon)A_{t,i}^{(b)}\Big)-\beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}\big[\phi_{\pi_{\theta}}\,\|\,\phi_{\pi_{\text{ref}}}\big]\Bigg].\end{split} (17) The expectation is taken over q ∼ 𝒟 q\sim\mathcal{D} and o t − 1 ∼ π θ old ( ⋅ ∣ q , o t ) o_{t-1}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(\cdot\mid q,\,o_{t}) for t = T , T − 1 , … , 1 t=T,T-1,\dots,1 and b = 1 , … , G b=1,\dots,G . Unlike the previous two variants, every token is supervised under the exact context in which it was generated, so the optimization landscape matches the inference-time denoising procedure step by step. This faithfulness comes at the cost of T T -fold more forward passes per response. Our method adapts the sequential masking variant by predicting the clean state 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} instead of 𝐱 t − 1 \mathbf{x}_{t-1} , retaining its trajectory-level precision at a fraction of the computational cost, thus striking a favorable balance between fidelity and efficiency.

sections.heading: Appendix B Reward Function
sections.text: For math tasks , we extract the content of the last \ \backslash boxed{...} from the model output and compare it against the ground truth via a math-equivalence check (combining string normalization, sympy -based symbolic comparison, and the math_verify library). The reward is binary: r math = { 1 , if ​ a ^ ≡ a ∗ 0 , otherwise r_{\mathrm{math}}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }\hat{a}\equiv a^{*}\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (18) where a ^ \hat{a} is the extracted answer and a ∗ a^{*} the ground truth. For code tasks , we extract the Python code block enclosed by ```python ``` and execute it against the provided unit tests in a sandboxed runner. The reward is the test-case pass rate: r code = # ​ passed test cases # ​ total test cases ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , r_{\mathrm{code}}=\frac{\#\,\text{passed test cases}}{\#\,\text{total test cases}}\in[0,1], (19) yielding a dense signal that rewards partial correctness and provides smoother gradients than the binary math reward.

sections.heading: C.1 Data Processing
sections.text: Out-of-memory (OOM) errors frequently occur during both rollout and training. To mitigate this, we restrict training data to subsets of the MATH and MBPP training splits with a maximum sequence length of 320 tokens for LLaDA and 256 tokens for Dream. Additionally, since binary rewards on MATH yield limited advantage diversity within each group, we retain only samples for which LLaDA produces at least one correct response across 16 generations, ensuring sufficient richness in the reward signal.

sections.heading: C.2 Remasking Strategy
sections.text: We adopt a sequential remasking strategy with weighted timestep sampling. The sampling temperature defined in Equation 6 is set at one. To balance training and rollout efficiency, we set k=16, meaning 16 timesteps are sampled per training example.

sections.heading: C.3 Training
sections.text: We use separate batch sizes for rollout and training. Prior to each training update, rollout responses are filtered to retain only samples exhibiting non-trivial policy gradients, i.e., those with varying reward values within a group. We apply a REINFORCE loss with a single gradient update per sample, rather than PPO. The KL penalty coefficient β \beta is set to 0.01 for LLaDA and 0.04 for Dream. The learning rate is fixed at 1 ​ e − 6 1e^{-6} throughout training.

sections.heading: C.4 Rollout
sections.text: A dynamic unmasking strategy is used for both rollout and evaluation. Tokens are unmasked greedily by highest probability when no token exceeds the confidence threshold of 0.9. To accelerate generation, we employ block-wise denoising with a block size of 32. LLaDA samples via the Gumbel-Max trick, adding Gumbel noise to logits and taking the argmax to implicitly approximate softmax sampling, with temperature controlling noise magnitude. Dream instead uses explicit categorical sampling, applying temperature scaling with optional top-p/top-k truncation before sampling from the softmax distribution. The rollout batch size is set to 8, with 4 generations per sample.

We introduce Reinforcement Learning from Denoising Feedback (RLDF) , a novel training paradigm that leverages feedback obtained from rollout and training processes to facilitate accurate and efficient policy loss estimation. To balance the trade-off between computational efficiency and estimation effectiveness, RLDF optimizes the model toward the clipped clean state x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} from intermediate noisy states x t x_{t} , combined with weighted timestep sampling over t t . Extensive experiments demonstrate that RLDF achieves consistent and substantial improvements in both performance and generalizability across two representative dLLM architectures, LLaDA and Dream, on multiple reasoning benchmarks. Our work lays a principled foundation for scalable reinforcement learning in diffusion language models. We build Drift , a training framework for dLLMs, available at https://github.com/ant-research/Drift . 1 Introduction Recent breakthroughs in diffusion language models (DLMs) ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) , such as Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) and LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) , have positioned them as a promising pathway toward highly capable foundation models ( Google DeepMind, 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Khanna et al., 2025 ) . The appeal of DLMs ( Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023 ; Yu et al., 2025b ) stems from several intrinsic advantages over autoregressive (AR) architectures: bidirectional attention ( Gong et al., 2025 ) , arbitrary decoding order, and the potential for multi-token parallel generation ( Wu et al., 2025b ; Wu et al., 2025a ) . Nevertheless, DLMs currently underperform their autoregressive counterparts across many benchmarks, a gap largely attributable to immature training methodologies and pipelines. Among the capabilities most in need of improvement, reasoning ( OpenAI, 2024 ; Anthropic, 2025 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) stands out as particularly critical. Reasoning of language models is a frontier that has been extensively explored and substantially advanced within the autoregressive paradigm. Reinforcement learning (RL) ( Kaelbling et al., 1996 ) has emerged as an effective and highly generalizable approach for cultivating reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs). Evolving from PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) through DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , and subsequent variants ( Yu et al., 2025a ; Yue et al., 2025 ) , RL has consistently improved LLM reasoning with verifiable reward ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Uesato et al., 2022 ) across diverse scenarios, including tool use ( Jin et al., 2025 ) , mathematics ( Snell et al., 2024 ) , and code generation ( Le et al., 2022 ; Shojaee et al., 2023 ) . However, these RL methods cannot be directly transplanted to diffusion language models due to two fundamental discrepancies: the attention mechanism (causal vs. bidirectional) and the generative process (next-token prediction vs. full-sequence denoising). A central obstacle in adapting RL to DLMs lies in policy loss estimation . In autoregressive models, the policy loss is obtained through a single forward pass under causal attention. In contrast, the arbitrary decoding order and bidirectional attention of DLMs render exact log-likelihood computation intractable. Prior approaches ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Ou et al., 2025 ) approximate the policy loss via either no-masking or random-masking schemes, both of which introduce a substantial mismatch between training and inference. Alternatively, computing the policy loss at every denoising step ( Ni et al., 2026 ) preserves train–inference alignment but incurs prohibitive computational and time costs due to the iterative nature of the denoising process. This exposes a core challenge: how to balance the fidelity of policy loss estimation against its computational cost. To address this challenge, we propose Reinforcement Learning from Denoising Feedback (RLDF) , a training paradigm that leverages two complementary feedback sources. Rollout feedback captures unmasking probabilities and their corresponding timesteps along the denoising trajectory. Training feedback , derived from predicted probabilities during denoising training, provides signals from which we retain only the most informative positions for stable and effective policy updates. Building on these signals, we employ a weighted sampling strategy ( Rubinstein and Kroese, 2016 ) that preferentially selects denoising steps with high predictive uncertainty ( Choi et al., 2022 ) —those exerting the greatest influence on the final generation. The policy loss is computed exclusively over these selected steps, yielding a favorable precision–efficiency trade-off while remaining compatible with diverse masking strategies and readily extensible to emerging training schemes. Empirical results demonstrate that our method exhibits substantial improvements on math and code tasks across both LLaDA and Dream models, as shown in Table 2 . Furthermore, our approach achieves faster convergence rates with more precise policy gradient estimation. We also demonstrate the advantage of leveraging the clean state rather than the next state for loss estimation, which avoids loss spikes and improves the utilization of training signals. In summary, our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We open-source Drift , an extensible and modular RL framework purpose-built for dLLMs, to facilitate community research and novel algorithms. • We propose an improved policy loss estimation method that achieves a better trade-off between efficiency and precision. • We unlock the reasoning potential of dLLMs (LLaDA and Dream), providing empirical insights for dLLM community. 2 Related Work 2.1 Diffusion Language Model Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have evolved significantly, spanning approaches from continuous ( Li et al., 2022 ; Dieleman et al., 2022 ) to discrete domains ( Hoogeboom et al., 2021 ) . Recently, masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) define a text generation paradigm in which the output is produced through an iterative denoising process over discrete token sequences ( Austin et al., 2021 ) . In contrast to autoregressive models, which generate tokens sequentially from left to right, dLLMs employ bidirectional attention mechanisms and perform predictions across all token positions at each forward pass. Recent advances in training methodology have yielded a number of capable dLLM foundation models, including LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) , which is trained from scratch via full pre-training, and Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , which is obtained by adapting the pretrained Qwen2.5-7B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) to the diffusion framework. 2.2 Reasoning in Diffusion Language Models Reasoning has long been a central topic in language model research. Diffusion language models have recently demonstrated promising potential across a range of reasoning tasks. The models show superiority in planning tasks ( Ye et al., 2024a ; Huang et al., 2025 ) and demonstrate better data learning efficiency ( Ni et al., 2025 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ) . Complementary lines of work have explored augmenting reasoning capabilities through established techniques such as chain-of-thought prompting ( Ye et al., 2024b ) , leveraging both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Austin et al., 2021 ) to elicit more structured and reliable inference. Further efforts have focused on accelerating the reasoning process ( Xie et al., 2025 ) , while others have investigated the design of remasking strategies to improve generation quality ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . 2.3 Reinforcement Learning Reinforcement learning (RL) ( Kaelbling et al., 1996 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) , especially GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , has proven effective in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) ( He et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2025 ) . However, owing to fundamental differences in attention mechanisms and forward computation processes, diffusion language models require distinct strategies for computing RL losses. Existing loss computation methods have undergone successive refinements, evolving from Diffu-GRPO ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) through Coupled-GRPO ( Xie et al., 2025 ) to ELBO ( Ou et al., 2025 ) , etc. Each of these methods attempts to better align the training objective with the denoising nature of diffusion models. Nevertheless, all of these methods suffer from training-inference mismatch to varying degrees, which undermines the reliability of policy gradient estimation and ultimately limits reasoning performance. We are motivated by this limitation and propose a novel loss computation method that considers both accuracy and efficiency, serving as a stronger foundation for reinforcement learning on diffusion language models. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 Forward and Denoising Process The forward process independently masks each token x 0 , i x_{0,i} with probability t t or leaves it unchanged with probability 1 − t 1-t , yielding the partially masked sequence x t x_{t} : q ⁡ ( x t ∣ x 0 ) = ∏ i = 1 L Cat ⁡ ( x t , i , ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝐞 x 0 , i + t ​ 𝐞 [MASK] ) . q(x_{t}\mid x_{0})=\prod_{i=1}^{L}\mathrm{Cat}\!\left(x_{t,i};\;(1-t)\,\mathbf{e}_{x_{0,i}}+t\,\mathbf{e}_{\texttt{[MASK]}}\right). (1) During denoising, dLLMs support both static and dynamic strategies. In static decoding, the model unmasks the top- k k most confident token positions at each step, where k k is a fixed hyperparameter. In dynamic decoding, tokens are unmasked based solely on predicted logits, with positions whose confidence exceeds a predefined threshold being unmasked at each step. To precisely describe the denoising process, we formalize the denoising process with the following definition. Given a prompt q q , let { o T , o T − 1 , … , o 0 } \{o_{T},o_{T-1},\ldots,o_{0}\} describe the denoising process, where T T is the number of denoising steps at inference time. Each o t o_{t} represents the model’s response state at denoising timestep t t . Specifically, o T o_{T} corresponds to the fully masked initial state, o 0 o_{0} denotes the final clean response, and intermediate states o t o_{t} ( 0 < t < T 0<t<T ) contain a mixture of decoded tokens and remaining mask tokens. 3.2 Training Techniques Following the masked language modeling paradigm of BERT, MDMs are trained via random masking. Specifically, a parametric model p θ ( ⋅ ∣ x t ) p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t}) takes the partially masked sequence x t x_{t} as input and simultaneously predicts all masked tokens (denoted as 𝙼 \mathtt{M} ). It is optimized via a cross-entropy loss computed exclusively over the masked positions: ℒ ( θ ) ≜ − 𝔼 t , x 0 , x t [ 1 t ∑ i = 1 L 𝟙 [ x t , i = 𝐌 ] log p θ ( x 0 , i ∣ x t ) ] . \mathcal{L}(\theta)\triangleq-\mathbb{E}_{t,\,x_{0},\,x_{t}}\left[\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\mathds{1}[x_{t,i}=\mathbf{M}]\log p_{\theta}(x_{0,i}\mid x_{t})\right]. (2) However, a fundamental discrepancy exists between the training and denoising processes. During training, masking is applied randomly and independently across token positions, whereas during denoising, the set of masked positions evolves deterministically across steps based on model confidence. This mismatch results in substantially different masking patterns and contextual inputs between the two phases, leading to inconsistent attention distributions and key-value representations. Such train-inference discrepancy poses a significant challenge for reasoning-oriented fine-tuning, as the model is optimized under a distribution of masked contexts that poorly reflects those encountered at inference time. 3.3 Challenges in Log Probability Estimation Unlike autoregressive models, whose loss can be computed within a single forward pass, diffusion language models do not enjoy this benefit due to their bidirectional attention mechanism. Specifically, the key-value (KV) representations change across denoising steps, making the forward computation distinct at each step. Early methods such as d1 ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) and wd1 ( Tang et al., 2025 ) adopt a full-sequence loss strategy, which computes the average loss over all token positions conditioned on the prompt only in a single forward pass: ℒ full-seq ​ ( o ∣ q ) = log ⁡ p θ ​ ( o ∣ q , o T ) . \mathcal{L}_{\text{full-seq}}(o\mid q)=\log p_{\theta}(o\mid q,o_{T}). (3) Subsequently, the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) was introduced, which approximates the log-likelihood via random masking over denoising timesteps: ℒ ELBO ​ ( o ∣ q ) = 𝔼 t , m ​ [ log ⁡ p θ ​ ( o ∣ q , o m ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\text{ELBO}}(o\mid q)=\mathbb{E}_{t,\,m}\left[\log p_{\theta}\big(o\mid q,\,o^{m}\big)\right], (4) where o m o^{m} denotes the response sequence randomly masked by ℳ \mathcal{M} . However, all of these methods compute the loss under a context that is inconsistent with the actual rollout conditions at inference time, giving rise to a fundamental training-inference mismatch that undermines the reliability of policy gradient estimation in RL training. 4 Reinforcement Learning from Denoising Feedback Figure 1: Comparison of training paradigms. Left: RL for autoregressive models without masking. Right: ELBO-based training for diffusion models with random masking. Bottom: Our proposed RLDF, which samples a timestep t and applies sequential masks. Policy loss is estimated based on π θ ​ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) \pi_{\theta}(x_{0}\mid x_{t}) . This formulation provides a more precise policy loss estimation while using identical trajectory context and objective. 4.1 Denoising Feedback of Diffusion Models The denoising process of diffusion models contains rich information that can substantially benefit reinforcement learning. We extract feedback from two complementary stages: the rollout process and the training process . During rollout, we collect reasoning trajectories together with their timestep probabilities, which capture the reasoning context and guide the timestep selection. During training, we predict the clean state x 0 x_{0} from the noisy state x t x_{t} and derive the learning signal from the processed x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} through token-level clipping. Both sources of feedback are effective in stabilizing training, yet have been largely overlooked in prior paradigms. 4.2 Loss Estimation at Timestep t To faithfully replicate the context in which each position is unmasked, we adopt a stepwise loss estimation scheme that enables precise gradient estimation without approximation. Formally, given a prompt q q and the sequence of tokens decoded across denoising timesteps o T , … , o 0 o_{T},\ldots,o_{0} , at each timestep t t we compute the forward process p ⁡ ( o 0 ∣ q , o t ) p(o_{0}\mid q,o_{t}) and evaluate the loss exclusively on the positions masked at timestep t t . This procedure exactly mirrors the model’s rollout without introducing any approximation error. However, this exact formulation incurs substantial computational overhead. Specifically, the number of forward passes scales linearly with the number of decoding steps n n , as the loss must be computed iteratively for each step. In practice, a standard reasoning trajectory requires approximately 256 decoding steps, resulting in 256 forward passes per sample and rendering naive stepwise training prohibitively expensive in both time and memory. Mathematical reasoning and code generation are widely adopted benchmarks for evaluating the reasoning capabilities of large language models. For mathematical reasoning, we use the official training split of MATH ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) for training, and evaluate on MATH500 ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) , GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , and AMC23 ( Art of Problem Solving, 2023 ) . Our reinforcement learning from denoising feedback (RLDF) method achieves consistently dominant performance across both LLaDA and Dream models on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, as reported in Table 2 . Nearly all configurations of our approach rank first or second among all baselines, with first-place results in the majority of settings. An unexpected finding is that the Dream model converges remarkably rapidly during reinforcement learning, requiring only approximately 100 training steps on both math and code tasks. Our reinforcement learning procedure effectively reactivates these dormant reasoning capacities, recovering and amplifying the model’s problem-solving abilities. We further observe that training on Dream exhibits greater instability compared to LLaDA, manifesting as rapidly escalating KL divergence; we address this by applying a higher KL penalty coefficient ( β = 0.04 \beta=0.04 ). As expected, increasing the number of sampling timesteps accelerates convergence, analogous to the effect of increasing batch size. Since each additional sampling timestep introduces an extra forward and backward pass, a larger number of timesteps directly increases per-iteration training time. In our implementation, using 16 sampling steps incurs a computation cost comparable to that of the rollout process alone. We further observe that the sampling temperature has a notable impact on training stability, with lower temperatures yielding more stable training dynamics. A higher temperature corresponds to a more uniform selection across timesteps, whereas a lower temperature biases sampling toward low-entropy timesteps. We attribute this, in part, to the behavior of loss estimation. High-entropy timesteps contain fewer tokens, but each token carries critical learning signal; however, their limited quantity makes the loss estimation inherently unstable. In contrast, low-entropy timesteps involve substantially more tokens, providing a larger collection for averaging, though they require probability-based filtering to isolate the informative training signal from low-value tokens. This reveals a signal-noise trade-off: sufficient signal is required for stable optimization, yet noise from low-entropy timesteps must not dominate the loss estimation. Consequently, choosing an appropriate probability filtering threshold is crucial for training stability. Figure 3: Ablation on sequential remasking strategy.
